newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet says executives got no 1996 bonus.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet says executives got no 1996 bonus.

text.p: ValuJet Inc's top executives received no bonuses in 1996, a reflection of the airline's poor financial performance last year, according to a regulatory filing.

"Due to the company's lack of profitabiliy during 1996, no bonuses were paid to the company's executive officers for the year," the Atlanta-based airline said in its annual proxy statement filed Wednesday with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

In 1996, the company lost $0.76 a share, or $41.5 million, on revenues of $219.6 million as a result of the company's forced shutdown after the May Flight 592 crash. That compares with a profit $1.13 a share, or $67.7 million, on revenues of $367.8 million in 1995.

As a result, the company's chairman and chief executive officer, Robert Priddy, received for 1996 a salary of $135,781, no bonus, no stock options and no other annual compensation, the low-cost carrier said.

Under the terms of a 1993 employment agreement, Priddy is to receive an annual salary of $150,000 through 1998, but his 1996 salary was lower because his pay was suspended when the airline was grounded after the Florida Everglades plane crash.
Lewis Jordan, president and chief operating officer, entered into a similar employment agreement, which set his pay at the same level.
Under the terms of their employment agreements, Priddy and Jordan are entitled to a bonus of up to two percent of the airline's pretax, pre-bonus income.
The company last month said it expects to report a "significant" loss in the first quarter, although it expects to return to profitability by the third quarter.
